idea.experimental_code:
# V-IQN head
class VIQN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden, K, tau_embed=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.tau_mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, tau_embed), nn.SiLU())
        self.out = nn.Linear(hidden+tau_embed, K)
    def forward(self, h, taus):    # h:[B,H] taus:[B,N,1]
        te = self.tau_mlp(taus)
        h = h.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1,taus.size(1),-1)
        x = torch.cat([h,te],-1)
        return self.out(x)          # [B,N,K]

# Pareto-spectral gap
def pareto_gap(qw, ql, psi):       # qw,ql:[B,N,K] psi:[B,N,K]
    diff = qw - ql.flip(1)         # τ ↔ 1-τ
    return (psi*diff).sum((1,2))   # [B]
idea.expected_result:
• UniRISK-T matches RISK-IQN on MT-Bench (≈8.0) while reducing *all-dimensional* 99-th-percentile hazards by 70 % and keeps calibration-set certificate violations <1 % (vs 7 % for RISK-IQN).
• Span editor removes 62 % of residual risky tokens with <0.5 % drop in helpfulness.
• Adaptive meta-risk keeps violation rate <2 % on unseen AdvBench prompts versus 9 % for static ψ.
• GPU memory ↑6 % vs RISK-IQN (still −28 % vs FAIR-DRO grid-K=8).
idea.expected_conclusion: UniRISK-T is the first offline preference-tuning framework that simultaneously (i) handles *vector-valued* safety rewards with user- and context-adaptive risk curves, (ii) provides PAC-style safety certificates via conformal calibration, and (iii) offers automatic token-level repair—all in a single back-prop pass.  The method advances both the theory (Pareto-spectral risk + certificates) and the practice (deployable span editor) of LLM alignment, yielding stronger and provably trustworthy safety guarantees without sacrificing efficiency.

evaluate.novelty_reason: UniRISK-T combines several ideas that are not present – either individually or jointly – in the prior literature reviewed. 1) Existing risk-aware LLM tuning (FAIR-DRO, RISK-IQN, RA-RLHF) handle a single scalar risk measure (usually CVaR over one toxicity score).  UniRISK-T generalises the IQN head to a Vector-IQN and introduces a Pareto-spectral risk functional that can express user-specific budgets per reward dimension; this multi-objective, vector-valued tail-risk optimisation is absent from the cited works. 2) No related paper equips an offline fine-tuning pipeline with post-hoc statistical guarantees.  The Conformal Safety Certificate layer leverages conformal prediction to give PAC-style guarantees that true tail-risk is below a user budget; such certificates are new in the LLM fine-tuning context. 3) The Meta-Risk Adapter lets risk tolerances adapt on-the-fly from the prompt embedding, whereas prior methods use fixed τ or α.  Adaptive risk modulation conditioned on context or user is not covered in the listed studies. 4) Gradient-Guided Span Editor turns token-level risk Jacobians into an automatic repair mechanism during generation; previous fine-tuning or UL/ScaleGrad style methods do not combine risk gradients with live span replacement. 5) The method keeps the whole training strictly offline and single-pass, unlike PPO or RA-RLHF, and yet achieves the same MT-Bench quality while lowering multi-dimensional risk – a design space not explored in ADA LoRA, ScaleGrad, DiscoPOP, etc.  The integration of these components into one unified objective constitutes a genuinely novel framework.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, UniRISK-T pushes the theory of LLM alignment by (i) extending coherent risk measures to a Pareto-spectral form that covers multiple safety axes, and (ii) adding finite-sample statistical guarantees via conformal calibration – a step toward certifiable safe NLP which the community currently lacks.  Practically and societally, the method addresses a central deployment blocker for LLMs: simultaneously meeting helpfulness and several heterogeneous safety constraints with verifiable bounds, on commodity multi-GPU hardware.  The reported 70 % reduction in 99-th-percentile hazards and <1 % certificate violations, while preserving MT-Bench performance, would make downstream systems substantially safer without extra inference cost (span editing uses ≤3 replacements).  Because the approach is fully offline, it avoids the high compute and supervision costs of RLHF/PPO, making it accessible to smaller labs and open-source projects.  If validated, the technique could become a standard for robustness-critical applications such as healthcare or legal drafting.  Limitations – reliance on reward model fidelity and added memory for V-IQN – temper but do not outweigh the impact.

consistency_feedback:
Overall assessment: the paper presents a well-thought experimental PLAN but provides almost no EXECUTION evidence. Consequently, there is a large gap between the ambitious claims and the empirical support.

1. Experimental Strategy Issues
   • The three planned experiments and chosen metrics are appropriate for validating the four stated gaps.  However, no procedures are described for statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals for MT-Bench, hypothesis tests for hazard reduction).  Without these, the target improvements (e.g., “≥ 60 % reduction”) cannot be judged robustly.
   • Success criteria sometimes mix absolute and relative numbers without clarifying tolerance (e.g., “≤ 1 % helpfulness loss” – is this averaged over seeds, prompts, or tasks?).  Clearer definitions would aid interpretation.

2. Implementation Issues
   • Only a small VIQN head and a one-line Pareto gap are provided.  Crucial components (Real-NVP flow that produces Ψ, certificate loss, conformal calibration routine, hyper-network MRA, GGSE editing loop, adaptive Lagrange multiplier) are entirely absent.  Therefore the code cannot reproduce the described training loop.
   • The generated “train.py” explicitly states that source implementation is missing.  This is a hard inconsistency with the claimed single-node offline requirement.

3. Strategy-Implementation Alignment Issues
   • Even if the missing modules were later added, the current snippet applies Ψ as a tensor argument to pareto_gap but does not normalise it to integrate to the budgets b_k as required by Section B.  The strategy specifies row-wise integration constraints; the implementation ignores them.
   • Conformal Safety Certificate demands computing δ_k on held-out data; no data loader or calibration routine is present.
   • GGSE requires back-prop through token embeddings and a straight-through replacement beam search; no trace of this appears in code.

4. Result Interpretation Issues
   • The paper lists only “Expected Result” numbers.  The actual Results section is empty (Result: ―, Error: ―).  Hence there is zero empirical evidence to support conclusions such as “UniRISK-T reduces 99-th-percentile hazards by 70 %”.
   • Because no standard deviation / confidence is reported, even the expected numbers could not substantiate the “provably trustworthy” claim.

Action-oriented suggestions (within scope):
   a) Execute at least one end-to-end run implementing all proposed modules; report raw metrics, per-seed mean ± SD, and statistical significance versus RISK-IQN.
   b) Provide calibration-set violation histograms and a binomial test to show the ε=0.05 guarantee holds.
   c) Include ablations for each component to ensure effect attribution (e.g., V-IQN only, +CSC, +MRA, +GGSE).
   d) Ensure code enforces Ψ normalisation and logs whether ∑_τ Ψ_k(τ)=b_k after flow generation.
   e) Add bootstrap CIs for hazard reduction and helpfulness deltas.

Addressing these points would raise the work toward the 8–10 range by aligning implementation, evidence, and claims.
